overview: Typhoid fever is a systemic bacterial infectious disease caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi. It is transmitted through contaminated food and water and remains a major public health concern in South Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Approximately 9.2 million typhoid cases occur globally each year, causing around 133,000 deaths. With appropriate antibiotic treatment, the case fatality rate drops below 1%, but rising drug resistance is a growing challenge.

types.name: Typhoid Fever (Enteric Fever)
types.description: Caused by Salmonella Typhi. Gradual onset with rising fever, abdominal symptoms, and risk of serious complications including intestinal perforation.

types.name: Paratyphoid Fever
types.description: Caused by Salmonella Paratyphi A, B, or C. Similar clinical presentation to typhoid but generally milder. No vaccine currently protects against paratyphoid.

types.name: Multidrug-Resistant (MDR) Typhoid
types.description: Strains resistant to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Particularly prevalent in South Asia.

types.name: Extensively Drug-Resistant (XDR) Typhoid
types.description: Strains resistant to fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, and multiple other antibiotics. Mainly treated with azithromycin (uncomplicated) or carbapenems (complicated). First reported in Pakistan (2016).

types.name: Chronic Typhoid Carrier State
types.description: 1–4% of patients continue to shed Salmonella Typhi in stool or urine for 12+ months after apparent recovery, often without symptoms, acting as long-term reservoirs of infection.

symptoms: Constipation (more common in adults) or diarrhea (more common in children)
Rose spots — faint pinkish rash on trunk (seen in some patients)
Relative bradycardia (slow heart rate relative to fever level)
causes: Ingestion of food or water contaminated with Salmonella Typhi from infected human feces
Consumption of raw fruits and vegetables washed with contaminated water
Eating food handled by chronic carriers without proper hand hygiene
Drinking untreated well or municipal water in endemic regions
Poor sanitation infrastructure allowing sewage to contaminate water supplies
risk_factors: Living in or travelling to South Asia (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh), Africa, or Latin America
Drinking untreated or poorly treated water
Eating street food or raw produce in endemic areas
Poor personal hygiene, especially inadequate handwashing
Young children and infants (higher risk of severe disease)
People taking acid-suppressing medications (PPIs reduce stomach acid defense against bacteria)
Close contact with a known typhoid case or carrier
Attending mass gatherings in endemic regions
diagnosis: Blood culture — gold standard (sensitivity ~50% single culture, higher with multiple)
Bone marrow culture — highest sensitivity (~80%), used when blood culture negative
Stool and urine cultures — useful in later stages of disease
Widal test — serological test, low reliability (poor sensitivity and specificity)
Typhidot / TUBEX tests — newer serology with variable reliability
PCR testing — rapid and sensitive, useful in research settings but not widely available
Clinical diagnosis — based on gradual fever progression, travel history, and symptoms

first_line_antibiotics: Ceftriaxone (IV) — for uncomplicated and complicated cases, widely used empirically
Azithromycin (oral) — for uncomplicated typhoid, effective against many resistant strains
Fluoroquinolones (Ciprofloxacin) — where susceptibility confirmed; resistance is common in South Asia
resistant_typhoid: Carbapenems (Meropenem, Imipenem) — for XDR typhoid or complicated cases unresponsive to other drugs
Azithromycin — preferred for XDR uncomplicated cases
supportive_care: Adequate hydration with oral or IV fluids
Nutritional support — small, frequent, easily digestible meals
Monitoring for and managing complications (perforation, haemorrhage)
surgical_management: Emergency surgery for intestinal perforation or haemorrhage
Bowel repair or resection depending on severity

complications: Intestinal perforation (most serious complication — occurs in ~1–3% of hospitalized cases)
Encephalopathy (typhoid toxin affecting brain — confusion, altered consciousness)
Relapse (up to 10% of treated patients — usually milder than initial illness)
prevention: Practice strict hand hygiene — wash hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet
Drink only clean, treated, or boiled water
Avoid raw produce that cannot be peeled or was washed in untreated water
Avoid street food or uncooked foods in endemic areas
Vaccination before travel to endemic regions
Improve sanitation and sewage infrastructure at community level
Identify and treat or monitor chronic carriers, especially those in food-handling roles
Ensure safe food handling practices — proper cooking and storage
emergency_signs: Sudden severe abdominal pain with rigid, board-like abdomen (suspect intestinal perforation)
Passing blood in stool or signs of severe internal bleeding
High fever persisting for more than 2–3 weeks despite treatment
Signs of shock — rapid weak pulse, cold clammy skin, very low blood pressure
Inability to drink fluids or persistent vomiting (risk of dehydration)

faqs.question: How is typhoid fever different from malaria?
faqs.answer: Both cause fever in tropical regions, but typhoid is bacterial (Salmonella Typhi, spread by contaminated food/water) while malaria is parasitic (Plasmodium, spread by mosquito bites). Typhoid typically has a gradual fever onset and abdominal symptoms, while malaria features cyclical chills and sweating. Blood culture confirms typhoid; blood smear or RDT confirms malaria.

faqs.question: Is the typhoid vaccine fully protective?
faqs.answer: No. Available vaccines offer 50–80% protection. The typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV) provides stronger, longer-lasting immunity especially in young children. No vaccine currently protects against paratyphoid fever. Food and water hygiene remain essential even after vaccination.

faqs.question: Can typhoid recur after treatment?
faqs.answer: Yes. Up to 10% of patients may experience relapse, usually within 2–3 weeks after apparent recovery. Relapse is generally milder. Completing the full antibiotic course reduces this risk.

faqs.question: What are chronic typhoid carriers?
faqs.answer: About 1–4% of typhoid patients become chronic carriers — they continue to shed bacteria in stool or urine for 12 months or more without feeling ill. Carriers can unknowingly spread infection, especially if they handle food. Prolonged antibiotic treatment (e.g., ciprofloxacin for 4 weeks) can sometimes clear the carrier state.
